title: Born Again to a Living Hope
summary: Peter praises God for new birth into a living hope, explains why faith is tested, and calls redeemed exiles to holiness and fervent love.
historicalContext: Peter writes a circular letter to congregations spread across five Roman provinces in northern and western Asia Minor, a vast region of cities, villages, and inland highlands. Most believers there had come from pagan backgrounds, though Jewish Christians shared their fellowship. Conversion had cost them socially. They withdrew from temple meals, civic festivals, and the moral customs inherited from their families, and neighbors answered with suspicion, slander, and informal pressure rather than any empire-wide decree. Peter, likely writing from Rome near the end of his life with Silvanus as his helper, addresses them with the vocabulary once reserved for Israel in dispersion. He reminds them that their estrangement is the consequence of belonging to God, that the Scriptures foresaw a pattern of suffering followed by glory, and that the Father who chose them will bring them safely to the inheritance He is keeping.
literaryContext: The chapter opens with a greeting (1:1-2) that already sounds the letter’s chief notes: election, exile, the Spirit’s sanctifying work, obedience, and the blood of Christ. A single sweeping sentence in Greek follows (1:3-12), blessing God for new birth, a guarded inheritance, joy amid trials, and a salvation searched out by prophets and watched by angels. With “Wherefore” in verse 13 Peter turns from what God has done to how His children must live. Four commands give the second half its spine: hope fully, be holy, pass your sojourn in reverent fear, and love one another fervently. Each command rests on a theological ground—the coming revelation of Christ, the holiness of the One who calls, the costly ransom of the Lamb, and the new birth through the abiding word. The closing quotation from Isaiah 40 frames everything in the contrast between fading flesh and the enduring word.
themes: New birth into a living hope through Christ’s resurrection
An inheritance kept in heaven and heirs guarded by God’s power
The prophets’ witness to Christ’s sufferings and glory
Holiness that reflects the God who calls
Redemption by the precious blood of the Lamb and love born of the enduring word

outline.title: Greeting to God’s Chosen Exiles
outline.summary: Peter addresses scattered believers as chosen by the Father, set apart by the Spirit, and brought into covenant through the obedience and sprinkled blood of Jesus Christ.

outline.title: A Living Hope Amid Trials
outline.summary: God is blessed for new birth into a living hope and a secure inheritance, while present trials prove faith that will be honored at Christ’s appearing.

outline.title: What Prophets Sought and Angels Watch
outline.summary: The salvation now preached was foretold by the Spirit of Christ through the prophets, who served later generations, and it remains a wonder to angels.

outline.title: Holy Children Redeemed at a Great Price
outline.summary: Believers are to set their hope on coming grace, imitate the holiness of God, and live in reverent fear because they were ransomed by the blood of Christ.

outline.title: Love Born of the Enduring Word
outline.summary: Those purified by obeying the truth and born again by God’s living word must love one another fervently, for human glory fades while the word abides.

verses.bibleText: Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, to the strangers scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The letter opens with a name that is itself a testimony. Simon, the fisherman from Bethsaida, writes under the name Jesus gave him, the Greek Petros, “stone.” The disciple who once tried to talk his Master out of the cross and who later denied Him in the high priest’s courtyard now writes as a restored servant. He claims no rank above the other apostles. “An apostle of Jesus Christ” means one sent with a message and bearing the authority of the One who sent him. The weight of what follows rests on Christ’s commission rather than on Peter’s personal prominence.

The readers are “strangers scattered.” Two Greek terms carry this address. Parepidēmoi describes people residing for a time in a place that is not their home. Diaspora was the word Greek-speaking Jews used for the covenant people dispersed among the nations after the exile. Peter applies both to congregations that were largely Gentile in origin (2:10; 4:3-4). Faith in Christ had made them aliens in their own towns. Their neighbors had not moved; their loyalties had. They now belonged to a homeland still ahead of them, and the festivals, customs, and moral assumptions of their surroundings no longer held the final claim on their lives.

The five regions named—Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia—cover most of the land north of the Taurus Mountains in what is now Turkey. Jews from several of these provinces heard Peter preach at Pentecost (Acts 2:9), and Paul was once prevented by the Spirit from entering Bithynia (Acts 16:7). The gospel had nevertheless taken root there, and the letter was evidently meant to travel from congregation to congregation across a wide territory.

The address already holds the shape of the whole letter. These believers are chosen by God and estranged from the world at once, and the two facts belong together. Christians who feel out of place in their culture need not conclude that something has gone wrong. Peter treats that tension as the normal condition of those whose citizenship is in heaven and who wait for the earth God will make new.

wordNotes.term: παρεπιδήμοις (parepidēmois) — strangers
wordNotes.explanation: The word describes a sojourner, someone living temporarily among a people not his own. Abraham used the related idea when he called himself a stranger among the Hittites. Peter applies it to believers whose permanent home is the inheritance God is keeping, so that their present residence, however long, is provisional.

wordNotes.term: διασπορᾶς (diasporas) — scattered
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “of the dispersion,” the term had long named Jewish communities living outside the land of promise. Peter extends it to the whole church in Asia Minor, presenting Gentile and Jewish believers alike as God’s covenant people living among the nations until He gathers them.

verses.bibleText: Elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, through sanctification of the Spirit, unto obedience and sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ: Grace unto you, and peace, be multiplied.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter describes his readers’ standing before God in three phrases, each naming one Person of the Godhead. The Father foreknows, the Spirit sanctifies, and the blood of the Son is sprinkled. The verse shows the Father, the Spirit, and Jesus Christ acting together in one saving work, each with a distinct part. Paul uses a similar pattern when he thanks God for believers chosen “through sanctification of the Spirit and belief of the truth” (2 Thessalonians 2:13).

“Elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father” places the origin of salvation in God’s initiative. Before these Asian believers ever heard the gospel, God knew them and purposed their salvation. Foreknowledge (prognōsis) in Scripture is more than awareness of future events; God’s knowing carries His loving regard and saving intention. Yet the passage gives no ground for an arbitrary decree that chooses some for life and passes others by without reference to their response. The same apostle says the Lord is “not willing that any should perish” (2 Peter 3:9). Election is in Christ and becomes effective as people hear the call and believe. Peter will soon describe his readers as those who “by him do believe in God” (1:21) and who purified themselves “in obeying the truth” (1:22). God foresees and welcomes that response without coercing it. His foreknowledge is the ground of their assurance, never a substitute for their faith.

“Through sanctification of the Spirit” names the means. The Holy Spirit sets apart those who receive the word, separating them from their former life and joining them to God’s holy people. The goal is “unto obedience and sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ.” The language recalls Sinai, where Israel pledged, “All that the LORD hath said will we do, and be obedient,” and Moses then sprinkled the blood of the covenant on the people (Exodus 24:7-8). Peter’s readers have entered the new covenant along the same lines of grace: a surrendered obedience to God and the cleansing of Christ’s shed blood applied to them. The blood covers those who come to God in submission, and the cleansed life is marked by willing obedience. Hebrews calls Christ the Mediator of the new covenant whose “blood of sprinkling” speaks better things than Abel’s (Hebrews 12:24), and it presents Him ministering the merits of that sacrifice in the heavenly sanctuary for His people.

The greeting “Grace unto you, and peace, be multiplied” is more than courtesy. People under pressure need an increasing measure of God’s favor and the settled peace of reconciliation with Him. Peter prays that these gifts will grow as the trials grow.

wordNotes.term: κατὰ πρόγνωσιν θεοῦ πατρός (kata prognōsin theou patros) — according to the foreknowledge of God the Father
wordNotes.explanation: The noun appears elsewhere in the New Testament only in Peter’s Pentecost sermon, where Christ is delivered up by God’s determinate counsel and foreknowledge, while those who crucified Him remain fully responsible. The same balance applies here: God’s foreknowledge establishes His gracious purpose without cancelling human response. In verse 20 the related verb describes Christ Himself, foreknown as the Lamb before the world began.

wordNotes.term: ῥαντισμὸν αἵματος (rhantismon haimatos) — sprinkling of the blood
wordNotes.explanation: The noun occurs elsewhere only in Hebrews. Sprinkled blood marked covenant ratification at Sinai and cleansing from defilement in the sanctuary services. Applied to Jesus Christ, it speaks of His sacrifice personally applied to believers, bringing forgiveness and admitting them to the privileges of the new covenant.

verses.bibleText: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, which according to his abundant mercy hath begotten us again unto a lively hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ” begins a single Greek sentence that runs to the end of verse 12. Before Peter says a word about suffering, he leads his readers into praise. The form recalls the Jewish blessing of God, now filled with new content: the God of Israel is known as the Father of Jesus the Messiah. Paul opens two letters with identical words (2 Corinthians 1:3; Ephesians 1:3), which suggests a phrase already at home in the worship of the early church.

The ground of praise is God’s “abundant mercy.” New birth is neither earned nor initiated by its recipients; it springs from the compassion of a God who sees human helplessness and acts. “Hath begotten us again” translates a verb found in the New Testament only here and in verse 23. It describes a beginning so complete that only birth can picture it. Jesus told Nicodemus that no one could see the kingdom without being born from above (John 3:3-5). Peter speaks of that new birth as God’s own act, by which He brings people into His family and makes them His children.

They are born “unto a lively hope.” The KJV’s “lively” means living. Many hopes in Peter’s world were dead ones, attached to idols that could not act, to rulers who would die, or to fortunes that could vanish in a night. The Christian hope is alive because it is fastened to a living Person. It comes “by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead.” Peter had looked into the empty tomb and met the risen Lord; his own hope had collapsed at the cross and revived on the third day. Christ’s rising is God’s proof that death does not have the final word, and it is the pledge that those who belong to Him will be raised at His coming (1 Corinthians 15:20-23).

A hope like this does not wait for circumstances to improve. Persecuted believers could lose property, reputation, and family ties, yet the event on which their hope rested lay beyond the reach of any magistrate. Anchored in a past resurrection and reaching toward a future one, it keeps a person moving forward when present conditions offer no reason for confidence.

wordNotes.term: ἀναγεννήσας (anagennēsas) — hath begotten us again
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to cause to be born anew. Peter uses it twice, here with the resurrection as the ground of the new birth and in verse 23 with the living word as its instrument. The image stresses divine parentage: the reborn receive a new life and a new Father, and with that a family likeness they are called to display.

wordNotes.term: ἐλπίδα ζῶσαν (elpida zōsan) — a lively hope
wordNotes.explanation: The participle “living” sets this hope against the empty expectations of those who are “without God in the world.” It is alive because its object, the risen Christ, is alive, and it is active, shaping conduct and endurance in the present.

verses.bibleText: To an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away, reserved in heaven for you,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The new birth leads “to an inheritance.” In Israel the inheritance was chiefly the land, each family’s allotment in Canaan received as a gift from God (Numbers 26:52-56). That inheritance could be seized by enemies, polluted by idolatry, and lost in exile. Peter describes a portion untouched by any of those threats, and he does so with three Greek adjectives that begin with the same sound: aphthartos, amiantos, amarantos.

It is “incorruptible”—death and decay cannot reach it. It is “undefiled”—no sin can stain it, as Israel’s land was once defiled by the very people who received it (Jeremiah 2:7). It “fadeth not away”—time does not dull its beauty, unlike the grass and flowers Peter will describe in verse 24. Taken together, the words declare that what God has prepared is permanent, pure, and always fresh.

The inheritance is “reserved in heaven for you.” The perfect tense pictures something placed under watch and kept there continually. It is as secure as the faithfulness of God. Jesus spoke of treasure laid up in heaven, where moth, rust, and thieves have no access (Matthew 6:19-20). Being reserved in heaven does not mean the inheritance will always remain remote from the earth. Scripture places its full possession on the renewed earth, where the meek inherit the land and God makes His dwelling with His people (Matthew 5:5; Revelation 21:1-3). Heaven is where it is kept; the new creation is where it will be enjoyed.

For readers who may have lost homes, standing, or family inheritance because of their faith, the verse sets a new value on what they possess. No court, mob, or relative can disinherit them from what God holds in trust.

wordNotes.term: ἄφθαρτον καὶ ἀμίαντον καὶ ἀμάραντον (aphtharton kai amianton kai amaranton) — incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away
wordNotes.explanation: Each adjective is formed with a negating prefix, giving the phrase a memorable ring. The first excludes decay, the second moral pollution, and the third the withering that overtakes living things. The same words describe the risen body, the holiness of Christ as High Priest, and the unfading crown promised to faithful shepherds.

wordNotes.term: τετηρημένην (tetērēmenēn) — reserved
wordNotes.explanation: The perfect passive participle describes something kept in the past and still being kept. God is the implied guardian, and the inheritance remains secure under His care until the day it is given.

verses.bibleText: Who are kept by the power of God through faith unto salvation ready to be revealed in the last time.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The inheritance is guarded in heaven, and the heirs are guarded on earth. “Who are kept by the power of God” uses a military verb for the garrison stationed to protect a town (2 Corinthians 11:32; Philippians 4:7). Over them God has posted a guard stronger than every hostile force.

The protection operates “through faith.” God’s power does the keeping, and faith is the means by which a person remains within that shelter. Faith does not supply the strength; it receives it. Two opposite errors are excluded: that a single past act of believing settles everything regardless of later choices, and that perseverance rests on human resolve. Peter places the believer’s security in God’s power, received and continued through trust. Whoever keeps looking to God remains under the garrison, while a person who abandons faith steps outside its protection (compare Jude 1:21, 24).

This keeping holds “unto salvation ready to be revealed in the last time.” Salvation has a present reality, but here Peter speaks of its completion. It is “ready” because Christ’s death, resurrection, and ascension have accomplished all that is needed, and it waits only for God’s appointed moment to be unveiled. That moment is the “last time,” the appearing of Jesus Christ (vv. 7, 13), when He returns personally and visibly, the dead in Christ are raised, and the redeemed are delivered from every trace of sin (1 Thessalonians 4:16-17).

Peter thus meets the anxious question whether believers can endure to the end. The God who keeps the inheritance for His people also keeps His people for the inheritance.

wordNotes.term: φρουρουμένους (phrouroumenous) — kept
wordNotes.explanation: The verb described soldiers guarding a city, either to keep enemies out or to keep inhabitants in. The present tense shows continuous protection. Paul uses it of God’s peace standing guard over hearts and minds in Christ Jesus.

wordNotes.term: ἐν καιρῷ ἐσχάτῳ (en kairō eschatō) — in the last time
wordNotes.explanation: Kairos denotes an appointed season rather than mere duration. The phrase points to the decisive moment when God brings history to its goal at the return of Christ, the same event Peter calls “the revelation of Jesus Christ.”

verses.bibleText: Wherein ye greatly rejoice, though now for a season, if need be, ye are in heaviness through manifold temptations:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Wherein ye greatly rejoice” looks back over the whole hope just described: new birth, a guarded inheritance, and a salvation ready to be revealed. The verb denotes exultant gladness, the kind Jesus urged on His persecuted followers when He told them to “be exceeding glad” (Matthew 5:12). Whether Peter is stating a fact or urging a habit, the joy is anchored in what God has secured rather than in present ease.

Beside the joy stands sorrow. “Though now for a season . . . ye are in heaviness” admits real grief. Peter does not ask his readers to deny pain or treat their losses as trivial. The two experiences coexist; a believer may weep and exult in the same week, even in the same hour. Three qualifiers set the grief in proportion. It is “now,” belonging to the present age. It lasts “for a season,” a little while measured against an unending inheritance. And it comes “if need be,” a phrase indicating that such trials are not random accidents. In a world where good and evil are locked in conflict, suffering for loyalty to Christ is to be expected, and God permits nothing He cannot bend toward His purposes.

The trials are “manifold,” many-colored, arriving in assorted forms: ridicule from neighbors, strained family ties, lost trade, illness, and the inner discouragement the enemy uses to wear down trust. James uses the same expression (James 1:2). Peter offers no catalog of afflictions, since his readers knew them well enough. He offers instead a vantage point from which any of them can be borne.

wordNotes.term: ἀγαλλιᾶσθε (agalliasthe) — ye greatly rejoice
wordNotes.explanation: This verb expresses exuberant, celebratory joy, frequently tied in Scripture to God’s saving acts. Mary uses it when her spirit rejoices in God her Saviour. Peter repeats it in verse 8, framing the mention of grief with joy on either side.

wordNotes.term: λυπηθέντες ἐν ποικίλοις πειρασμοῖς (lypēthentes en poikilois peirasmois) — in heaviness through manifold temptations
wordNotes.explanation: The participle describes being grieved or distressed. Poikilos means varied or multicolored, and peirasmos here refers to trials that test loyalty rather than enticements to sin. The pairing honestly acknowledges sorrow while placing it inside a larger hope.

verses.bibleText: That the trial of your faith, being much more precious than of gold that perisheth, though it be tried with fire, might be found unto praise and honour and glory at the appearing of Jesus Christ:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter now states the purpose behind the trials: “that the trial of your faith . . . might be found unto praise and honour and glory.” The word translated “trial” refers to what remains after testing, the proven quality of faith. To illustrate, Peter reaches for the most precious metal his readers knew. Gold was refined by heat. The ore was melted, the dross skimmed off, and the pure metal left behind. Faith passes through a similar fire.

Peter then adds an unexpected turn. Gold “perisheth,” even after refining. It is valuable, yet it belongs to the order of things that will pass away, and in the end it will be consumed with the rest of the present world (2 Peter 3:10). Faith that has endured testing is “much more precious” because it outlasts every earthly treasure and leads to life without end. If people willingly put gold through the furnace to prove and purify it, God’s dealings with the faith of His children are hardly cruel. He prizes that faith more than any refiner prizes his metal, and He sits beside the crucible watching (Malachi 3:3).

The outcome will be displayed “at the appearing of Jesus Christ.” The word is apokalypsis, the unveiling of One now hidden from sight. At His return the tested faith of believers will be brought into the open and will result in “praise and honour and glory.” This is first the praise of God, whose grace sustained that faith, and it includes the commendation He gives His servants: “Well done” (Matthew 25:21). The reward is not wages earned by suffering. It is the Lord’s public acknowledgment of what His grace produced in people who kept trusting Him.

Trials therefore need not be read as signs that faith is failing. Peter presents them as the process that reveals faith’s worth and strengthens it. A believer in the furnace can know that the fire has limits and that the Refiner has a purpose.

wordNotes.term: τὸ δοκίμιον ὑμῶν τῆς πίστεως (to dokimion hymōn tēs pisteōs) — the trial of your faith
wordNotes.explanation: The noun can denote either the testing process or the tested, approved result. Here the accent falls on the result: faith shown to be real and valuable after it has been tried. The image belongs to the refiner’s craft, which Scripture often applies to God’s purifying of His people.

wordNotes.term: ἐν ἀποκαλύψει Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ (en apokalypsei Iēsou Christou) — at the appearing of Jesus Christ
wordNotes.explanation: Apokalypsis means an unveiling. Applied to Christ, it points to His personal return in glory, when the One now unseen will be revealed to all. Peter uses the phrase again in verse 13 and in chapter 4, always tying present endurance to that coming day.

verses.bibleText: Whom having not seen, ye love; in whom, though now ye see him not, yet believing, ye rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
From the faith being tested Peter turns to the Person in whom that faith rests. “Whom having not seen, ye love.” Peter himself had seen Jesus. He had walked the roads of Galilee with Him, eaten with Him, and heard Him ask three times beside the lake, “Lovest thou me?” (John 21:15-17). His readers had never laid eyes on the Lord, yet they loved Him. The apostle does not treat their love as inferior to his own. Jesus had pronounced a blessing on those “that have not seen, and yet have believed” (John 20:29).

The verse sets two pairs side by side: not having seen, yet loving; not seeing now, yet believing. Faith and love here are personal, directed toward Christ Himself and sustained through prayer, the Scriptures, and the presence of His Spirit. Christian life in this age is a walk “by faith, not by sight” (2 Corinthians 5:7), and the word “now” implies that the time of not seeing will end. He will be seen face to face.

The result is “joy unspeakable and full of glory.” The joy exceeds what words can express, and it is glorified, already touched by the splendor that will be revealed. The full experience of glory belongs to the day of Christ’s appearing, but the believer tastes it beforehand in communion with the unseen Lord (compare 4:14). Because this joy springs from relationship with Christ rather than from outward conditions, it can coexist with the heaviness Peter admitted in verse 6.

wordNotes.term: χαρᾷ ἀνεκλαλήτῳ καὶ δεδοξασμένῃ (chara aneklalētō kai dedoxasmenē) — joy unspeakable and full of glory
wordNotes.explanation: The first adjective, found only here in the New Testament, means inexpressible. The second is a perfect participle, “glorified,” describing joy already permeated by the glory of the age to come. Present gladness is a foretaste of future vindication.

verses.bibleText: Receiving the end of your faith, even the salvation of your souls.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The joy of verse 8 is grounded in what believers are “receiving.” The present participle shows them already beginning to obtain “the end of your faith.” The word telos means goal or outcome. Faith is never an end in itself; it reaches toward salvation, and that salvation is both a present possession and a future completion. Those who trust Christ already know forgiveness, the Spirit’s renewing work, and fellowship with God, while full deliverance awaits the appearing of Christ named in verses 5 and 7.

“The salvation of your souls” should be heard in its biblical sense. The Greek psychē often denotes a person’s life or whole self, as when Jesus warned that whoever would save his life must lose it for His sake (Matthew 16:25). Peter is not setting an immortal inner part against a perishable body. He speaks of the deliverance of the entire person, a salvation that will be complete when the dead in Christ rise and the living are changed at His coming (1 Corinthians 15:51-53). The inheritance of verse 4, Eden restored on a renewed earth, is the destination toward which faith presses.

wordNotes.term: τὸ τέλος τῆς πίστεως (to telos tēs pisteōs) — the end of your faith
wordNotes.explanation: Telos signifies the goal toward which something moves and the outcome it reaches. Paul uses it of the end of sanctification, everlasting life. Faith’s goal is salvation in its fullness.

wordNotes.term: σωτηρίαν ψυχῶν (sōtērian psychōn) — the salvation of your souls
wordNotes.explanation: In biblical usage psychē frequently means the living person or one’s life, beginning with the man who became “a living soul” at creation. The phrase therefore points to the rescue of the whole self, completed at the resurrection, rather than to the escape of a detached inner essence.

verses.bibleText: Of which salvation the prophets have enquired and searched diligently, who prophesied of the grace that should come unto you:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter now carries his readers back to the prophets. “Of which salvation the prophets have enquired and searched diligently.” Both verbs are intensive: they sought out, and they searched out with care. Inspired men such as Isaiah, Daniel, and Zechariah did not receive revelation and then set it aside. They studied what God had shown them and what He had given to other prophets, comparing message with message to grasp the outline of His plan. Daniel, for instance, examined Jeremiah’s prophecy of seventy years and then prayed for further light (Daniel 9:2-3).

Their subject was “the grace that should come unto you.” The KJV supplies the words “that should come,” but the sense is plain: the prophets spoke of a grace intended for a later generation. The gracious purpose of God revealed in Jesus Christ was no novelty invented in Peter’s day. It had been announced, longed for, and searched out across centuries.

This gives Peter’s readers a lineage. Gentile converts in remote provinces might appear to be latecomers to the story of God. In fact they stood at the very point toward which Israel’s prophets had strained to look. Jesus told His disciples that many prophets and righteous men had desired to see what they were seeing (Matthew 13:17). The persecuted believers of Asia Minor shared that privilege, and their faith rested on a word far older than the empire that troubled them.

wordNotes.term: ἐξεζήτησαν καὶ ἐξηρεύνησαν (exezētēsan kai exēreunēsan) — have enquired and searched diligently
wordNotes.explanation: Both verbs carry a prefix that intensifies the action, describing a thorough and persistent investigation. The prophets were active students of revelation, not passive channels, and their diligence models the careful searching of Scripture that Jesus commended.

verses.bibleText: Searching what, or what manner of time the Spirit of Christ which was in them did signify, when it testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ, and the glory that should follow.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
What did the prophets want to know? They were “searching what, or what manner of time” the Spirit was indicating. The phrase could mean “what person or what time,” but more likely it doubles the interest in time for emphasis: when, and under what circumstances, would these things come to pass? Scripture shows prophets asking exactly such questions. Daniel asked, “How long shall it be to the end of these wonders?” and was told the words were sealed until the time of the end (Daniel 12:6-9). They knew enough to be certain of the events and not enough to settle every detail of their timing, a condition the church shares as it looks for Christ’s return.

The revealing agent was “the Spirit of Christ which was in them.” The phrase is remarkable. The Spirit who moved Israel’s prophets is called the Spirit of Christ, which implies that Christ existed and was active long before Bethlehem. The prophets did not speak from personal insight or national ambition; the Spirit worked within their minds and testified through them (2 Peter 1:21). Peter will build on this truth in 3:18-20, where Christ, by the Spirit, preached through Noah to the people of his day. Whether the phrase means the Spirit sent by Christ or the Spirit through whom Christ Himself was present, it affirms both Christ’s deity and the divine origin of the Old Testament.

The Spirit “testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ, and the glory that should follow.” The sequence matters. Isaiah 53 portrays a Servant wounded and then exalted. Psalm 22 moves from forsakenness to praise among the nations. Psalm 118 speaks of a rejected stone made the head of the corner, a text Peter will quote in chapter 2. The risen Jesus opened these Scriptures to His disciples: “Ought not Christ to have suffered these things, and to enter into his glory?” (Luke 24:26). The Greek plural, “glories,” may embrace the resurrection, the ascension, His heavenly ministry, and the coming kingdom.

Suffering followed by glory is the thread that runs through the entire letter. What was true of the Head will be true of the body. Believers who suffer for Christ’s name walk the road He walked and may expect the glory that followed for Him (4:13; 5:1).

wordNotes.term: τὸ ἐν αὐτοῖς πνεῦμα Χριστοῦ (to en autois pneuma Christou) — the Spirit of Christ which was in them
wordNotes.explanation: Paul uses the same title for the Holy Spirit who indwells believers. Applied to the prophets, it identifies the Spirit who inspired the Old Testament with the Spirit of the risen Lord, and it presupposes Christ’s existence and activity before the incarnation.

wordNotes.term: τὰ εἰς Χριστὸν παθήματα καὶ τὰς μετὰ ταῦτα δόξας (ta eis Christon pathēmata kai tas meta tauta doxas) — the sufferings of Christ, and the glory that should follow
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “the sufferings destined for Christ and the glories after these.” The phrase summarizes the messianic pattern foretold in the prophets: humiliation first, exaltation after. Peter applies the same order to the experience of Christ’s followers.

verses.bibleText: Unto whom it was revealed, that not unto themselves, but unto us they did minister the things, which are now reported unto you by them that have preached the gospel unto you with the Holy Ghost sent down from heaven; which things the angels desire to look into.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The prophets learned something about the reach of their own work: “not unto themselves, but unto us they did minister.” The better-attested reading has “unto you,” addressing Peter’s readers directly. The prophets served their own generation with rebuke, comfort, and instruction, yet they also understood that the fulfillment of their central promises lay beyond their lifetimes. Their writings were a service rendered in advance to people who would live after the Messiah came. Paul says much the same of Israel’s history, that it was written “for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the world are come” (1 Corinthians 10:11).

That message has now been “reported unto you by them that have preached the gospel unto you with the Holy Ghost sent down from heaven.” The Spirit who spoke in the prophets came in power at Pentecost and now fills the evangelists. The prophets foretold, the preachers announced fulfillment, and one Spirit stood behind both. This unity explains why Peter can quote Leviticus, Isaiah, and the Psalms throughout his letter as God’s word to Christians. The Old Testament and the apostolic gospel form a single testimony to Christ.

The verse closes with a striking line: “which things the angels desire to look into.” The verb means to stoop and peer, the same word used when Peter and John bent down to look into the empty tomb (Luke 24:12; John 20:5). Holy angels, who never needed redemption, watch the plan of salvation with intense interest. In it the character of God, His justice and His mercy together, is displayed before the universe in a way that answers every accusation raised against Him in the great controversy with evil. The cross reveals a love that angels study and celebrate (Ephesians 3:10).

Peter’s readers, despised in their own towns, are therefore part of a drama watched from heaven. The gospel they had received was searched out by prophets and gazed upon by angels.

wordNotes.term: παρακύψαι (parakypsai) — to look into
wordNotes.explanation: The verb pictures someone bending over to peer closely at something, as the disciples and Mary did at the tomb. James uses it of looking intently into the perfect law of liberty. Here it conveys the eager, sustained attention of angels to the unfolding of redemption.

wordNotes.term: διηκόνουν (diēkonoun) — they did minister
wordNotes.explanation: The imperfect tense describes ongoing service. The prophets acted as servants whose ministry extended past their own era, supplying later believers with the testimony that now confirms the gospel.

verses.bibleText: Wherefore gird up the loins of your mind, be sober, and hope to the end for the grace that is to be brought unto you at the revelation of Jesus Christ;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Wherefore” turns the letter from praise to direction. Everything in verses 3-12—the new birth, the guarded inheritance, the tested faith, the testimony of prophets—now becomes the reason for a way of life. The first command is to hope, and the two clauses that precede it describe how hope is kept steady.

“Gird up the loins of your mind.” A traveler or laborer in a long robe would gather it up and tuck it into his belt so it would not hinder his stride. Israel ate the first Passover with loins girded, ready to march out of Egypt (Exodus 12:11), and Jesus told His disciples to keep their loins girded and their lamps burning as they waited for their Lord (Luke 12:35). Peter applies the picture to the mind. Believers are to gather their scattered thoughts, lay aside idle and unprofitable speculation, and make ready for disciplined action. With this comes “be sober,” a call to clear-headed watchfulness that refuses every kind of intoxication, whether by wine, by fear, or by the excitements of the surrounding culture (compare 4:7; 5:8).

The main verb follows: “hope to the end.” The adverb may belong with “be sober” or with “hope,” but the thrust is a hope set wholly and without reserve. Divided hope, resting partly on Christ and partly on circumstances, will falter under pressure. Its object is “the grace that is to be brought unto you at the revelation of Jesus Christ.” Grace has already been received, yet its fullness is still to come, carried to believers when Christ appears. The present participle, “is being brought,” suggests that grace is already on its way.

Hope in Scripture is never mere wishful thinking. It is confident expectation grounded in what God has already done, and it governs how a person thinks and acts in the meantime. Those who will greet Christ with joy at His appearing are the ones learning to know and trust Him now.

wordNotes.term: ἀναζωσάμενοι τὰς ὀσφύας τῆς διανοίας (anazōsamenoi tas osphyas tēs dianoias) — gird up the loins of your mind
wordNotes.explanation: To gird the loins was to bind up a flowing garment for vigorous movement. Joined to dianoia, the faculty of thought and understanding, the idiom calls for a mind gathered, focused, and ready for action. The aorist participle presents this readiness as a decisive preparation underlying the command to hope.

wordNotes.term: νήφοντες (nēphontes) — be sober
wordNotes.explanation: Originally the verb meant to abstain from wine. In the New Testament it consistently describes mental and spiritual alertness, a balanced and watchful frame of mind. Peter repeats the call twice more, each time in connection with prayer and resistance to the devil.

verses.bibleText: As obedient children, not fashioning yourselves according to the former lusts in your ignorance:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter grounds his second command in identity. His readers are “obedient children,” literally “children of obedience,” a Hebrew way of describing people marked by a defining quality, much as “children of wrath” and “children of light” do elsewhere (Ephesians 2:3; 5:8). The new birth of verse 3 has made them God’s children, and the family trait is a willing response to the Father’s will. The phrase echoes the “obedience” of verse 2.

Accordingly they are not to be “fashioning yourselves according to the former lusts.” The verb, used elsewhere in the New Testament only in Romans 12:2, means to take on the shape of a pattern. Before conversion their lives had been molded by desires that ruled them. Peter calls that period one of “ignorance,” meaning they did not know God, His law, or His Son (Acts 17:30; Ephesians 4:17-18). Their earlier way of living had seemed normal, even respectable, to everyone around them.

Peter recognizes that old patterns pull hard. Newly converted Gentiles lived among friends and relatives who still practiced what they had left behind, and the temptation to slide back into familiar ways was constant. Refusing the old mold is only half of Peter’s answer. The other half follows in verse 15: taking on the shape of a new pattern, the character of the Father whose children they have become. The grace that changed their standing also reshapes their conduct.

wordNotes.term: ὡς τέκνα ὑπακοῆς (hōs tekna hypakoēs) — as obedient children
wordNotes.explanation: The Semitic idiom “children of” a quality identifies that quality as characteristic. Believers are those whose lives are defined by obedience to God, a trait that grows from the new birth rather than producing it.

wordNotes.term: μὴ συσχηματιζόμενοι (mē syschēmatizomenoi) — not fashioning yourselves
wordNotes.explanation: The verb describes conforming oneself to an external pattern. The present tense forbids an ongoing practice: believers must stop letting their former desires press them into the old shape.

verses.bibleText: But as he which hath called you is holy, so be ye holy in all manner of conversation;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The positive standard follows: “as he which hath called you is holy, so be ye holy.” God’s call in this letter is effective; it summoned these people “out of darkness into his marvellous light” (2:9). The One who called them is holy, and His character sets the pattern for theirs. In Scripture holiness begins with God Himself: utterly pure, separate from all evil, and majestic in moral beauty. Isaiah heard the seraphim cry “Holy, holy, holy” and was overwhelmed by his own uncleanness (Isaiah 6:3-5).

To be holy is to belong to God and to reflect His character. Both ideas are present—separation from what defiles and likeness to the One who is pure. Humanity was created in God’s image (Genesis 1:26-27), and sin defaced that likeness. The gospel aims to restore it. Holiness is therefore no external code bolted onto Christian life; it is the recovery of what human beings were made to be.

The scope is “all manner of conversation.” In the KJV “conversation” means conduct, a person’s entire manner of life. Holiness is not confined to worship, sacred seasons, or religious acts. It reaches into business dealings, speech, family relationships, eating and drinking, recreation, and the use of time and money. No region of life lies outside the claim of the holy God. The aorist imperative suggests a decisive commitment: let holiness become the settled character of every part of your conduct.

wordNotes.term: ἅγιοι ἐν πάσῃ ἀναστροφῇ (hagioi en pasē anastrophē) — holy in all manner of conversation
wordNotes.explanation: Anastrophē, a favorite word of Peter’s, refers to one’s whole way of life and behavior. Paired with “all,” it extends holiness to every sphere of daily existence. Paul prays similarly that God would sanctify believers wholly.

verses.bibleText: Because it is written, Be ye holy; for I am holy.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter supports the command with Scripture: “Because it is written, Be ye holy; for I am holy.” For the apostles, “it is written” settled a question. The words come from Leviticus, where they occur several times (11:44-45; 19:2; 20:7, 26). God spoke them to Israel, and Peter applies them without hesitation to believers in Asia Minor, many of them Gentiles. This is the principle of verse 12 at work: Moses and the prophets ministered to later generations, and God’s word to Israel remains His word to the church.

The settings of the command in Leviticus are instructive. In chapter 11 it closes the instruction distinguishing clean from unclean animals for food; God’s people were to display their holiness even at the table. In chapter 19 it introduces a wide-ranging series of commands: reverence for parents, keeping the Sabbath, leaving gleanings for the poor, honest dealing, refusing to slander, and loving one’s neighbor as oneself (Leviticus 19:3, 9-18). In chapter 20 it stands against occult practices and sexual immorality. Holiness in Leviticus thus covers worship, diet, family, economics, speech, and sexuality, which matches the breadth of Peter’s “all manner of conversation” in verse 15.

The reason given is God’s own character: “for I am holy.” The command does not rest on social usefulness or community approval. God’s people are to be holy because they belong to Him and bear His name. What He is, He calls them to become. What He commands, He also supplies: “I am the LORD which sanctify you” (Leviticus 20:8). The holiness He requires is the holiness He produces through His Spirit (v. 2), so that the call becomes a promise as well as a duty.

wordNotes.term: ἅγιοι ἔσεσθε, ὅτι ἐγὼ ἅγιος (hagioi esesthe, hoti egō hagios) — Be ye holy; for I am holy
wordNotes.explanation: Manuscripts vary between the imperative “be holy” and the future “ye shall be holy,” the form found in the Greek translation of Leviticus. The future in a divine command functions as an imperative while also carrying the force of a promise. Either way, the standard and the ground of holiness lie in the nature of God Himself.

verses.bibleText: And if ye call on the Father, who without respect of persons judgeth according to every man's work, pass the time of your sojourning here in fear:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The third command concerns the believer’s posture during the present pilgrimage. “If ye call on the Father” assumes that the readers do pray to God as Father; the condition expresses fact, not doubt. That privilege, the intimacy Jesus taught in the prayer “Our Father which art in heaven,” brings responsibility with it. The Father they address is also the Judge.

He “without respect of persons judgeth according to every man’s work.” The rare adverb means without receiving the face, that is, without favoritism (Acts 10:34; Romans 2:11). Being God’s child grants no exemption from His evaluation. Scripture consistently teaches a judgment that weighs every life, believers included (2 Corinthians 5:10; Ecclesiastes 12:14), and the Father carries it out through the Son (John 5:22). “Work” is singular here: the whole pattern of a life viewed as one, the conduct that shows whether faith was living. This does not make salvation a reward for works. It recognizes that saving faith expresses itself in works and that God’s judgment will make that evident.

The fitting response is to “pass the time of your sojourning here in fear.” The word for sojourning describes residence as a foreigner, recalling the “strangers” of verse 1. Earth is the place of their temporary stay. “Fear” in this setting means reverence, a sober awareness of who God is and what one’s conduct means to Him. It differs from the dread of a tyrant. It resembles the respect of a child who loves his father and has no wish to grieve him.

Reverence toward God also frees believers from the fear of people (3:14-15). Those who stand in awe of the impartial Judge are not easily intimidated by the slander of their neighbors.

wordNotes.term: ἀπροσωπολήμπτως (aprosōpolēmptōs) — without respect of persons
wordNotes.explanation: Formed from the idiom “to receive a face,” meaning to show partiality, this adverb appears only here in the New Testament. God’s judgment is not swayed by status, nationality, or religious privilege. James applies the same principle to the conduct of believers toward the poor.

wordNotes.term: τὸν τῆς παροικίας ὑμῶν χρόνον (ton tēs paroikias hymōn chronon) — the time of your sojourning
wordNotes.explanation: Paroikia denotes living as a resident alien. Luke uses it of Israel’s stay in Egypt, a period that ended in redemption. Peter’s readers likewise live as aliens until God brings them home.

verses.bibleText: Forasmuch as ye know that ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold, from your vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Reverence rests on knowledge: “Forasmuch as ye know that ye were not redeemed with corruptible things.” To redeem meant to release by payment of a ransom. Peter’s readers knew the practice well. Captives of war were ransomed, slaves could be freed when a price was paid, and in Israel a kinsman might buy back a relative’s land or person (Leviticus 25:47-49). The Old Testament also spoke of God redeeming His people from Egypt by His outstretched arm (Exodus 6:6; Deuteronomy 7:8).

The price was not “silver and gold.” Those metals were the ordinary currency of ransom, and Peter has already said that gold perishes (v. 7). Nothing perishable could pay for a deliverance meant to last forever. Isaiah had promised that God’s people would be redeemed “without money” (Isaiah 52:3).

The bondage from which they were freed is “your vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers.” “Vain” means empty and futile, leading nowhere. The ancient world revered ancestral custom as the foundation of a stable society, and to abandon the ways of one’s fathers was viewed as disloyal and dangerous. Peter boldly calls that inherited way of life futile. The idols, festivals, and moral habits handed down through generations could give neither life nor hope. The description fits Gentile converts most naturally, though any tradition that substitutes human custom for the word of God falls under the same verdict (Mark 7:7-8).

Here lies one reason Peter’s readers were resented: redemption had required them to break with family tradition. Peter does not soften that break; he explains it. Christ paid far too much for their freedom for them to drift back into the bondage they had left.

wordNotes.term: ἐλυτρώθητε (elytrōthēte) — ye were redeemed
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to set free by paying a ransom. The passive voice points to God as the Redeemer. In the Greek Old Testament it describes the exodus, and in the New Testament it describes Christ giving Himself to free a people for God.

wordNotes.term: ματαίας ἀναστροφῆς πατροπαραδότου (mataias anastrophēs patroparadotou) — vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers
wordNotes.explanation: Mataios describes what is empty or useless, a word Scripture often applies to idolatry. The compound adjective means “handed down from ancestors.” Together they portray an inherited way of life that looked venerable but proved futile.

verses.bibleText: But with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The contrast with silver and gold is sharp: “But with the precious blood of Christ.” “Precious” means costly, of immense value. Gold has a market price; the blood of Christ has a worth no market could set. Blood in Scripture represents life surrendered in death (Leviticus 17:11), so Christ’s blood means His life poured out at Calvary, the death by which sinners are ransomed (Mark 10:45).

He is “as of a lamb without blemish and without spot.” The image draws on Israel’s sacrificial system and above all on the Passover. At the exodus each household chose a lamb “without blemish” (Exodus 12:5), slew it, and put its blood on the doorposts; the destroyer passed over, and Israel went out free. Every sacrifice brought to the sanctuary had to be free of defect (Leviticus 22:19-21). Those physical requirements pointed beyond themselves to the moral perfection of the One who would fulfill them. John the Baptist introduced Jesus as “the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world” (John 1:29), and Paul calls Him “our passover” sacrificed for us (1 Corinthians 5:7).

The two adjectives stress sinlessness. Only a sinless substitute could die for the guilt of others rather than His own. Peter, who lived beside Jesus for three years, testifies that He “did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth” (2:22). Christ’s perfect obedience gives His death its saving value, and His blood, presented in the heavenly sanctuary where He ministers as High Priest, is the ground of the believer’s forgiveness and access to God (Hebrews 9:12-14).

The redemption Peter describes is a new exodus. As Israel was freed from Egyptian slavery by the blood of a lamb and led toward an inheritance, so believers are freed from a futile way of life by the blood of Christ and are journeying toward the inheritance kept in heaven. The cost of their deliverance shows what they are worth to God, and it gives every reason to live in reverent gratitude.

wordNotes.term: τιμίῳ αἵματι (timiō haimati) — the precious blood
wordNotes.explanation: Timios means of great price or highly valued. Set against perishable silver and gold, it underlines the infinite worth of Christ’s sacrifice. Scripture ties atonement to blood because the life is in the blood, and the redeemed in heaven sing that Christ purchased them by it.

wordNotes.term: ἀμνοῦ ἀμώμου καὶ ἀσπίλου (amnou amōmou kai aspilou) — a lamb without blemish and without spot
wordNotes.explanation: Amōmos was the technical term for a sacrificial animal free from defect; aspilos means unstained. Applied to Christ, the pair moves from ritual fitness to moral purity, presenting Him as the sinless offering foreshadowed by the Passover lamb.

verses.bibleText: Who verily was foreordained before the foundation of the world, but was manifest in these last times for you,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter now sets the cross within God’s eternal purpose. Christ “verily was foreordained before the foundation of the world.” The verb is the cognate of “foreknowledge” in verse 2. Before creation, God knew and purposed the gift of His Son as the Lamb. The plan of redemption was no emergency measure improvised after Eden. Revelation speaks of “the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world” (Revelation 13:8), and Paul of a mystery “kept secret since the world began” and now made known (Romans 16:25-26).

The same word links Christ with His people. Believers are elect according to God’s foreknowledge (v. 2), and Christ was foreknown as their Redeemer. Their election rests in His. God did not foreknow a people apart from a Saviour; He foresaw both together in one gracious design.

“But was manifest in these last times for you.” What lay hidden in God’s purpose became visible in history. The verb “manifest” implies prior existence: One who already was appeared among men (1 Timothy 3:16; 1 John 1:2). The incarnation, life, death, and resurrection of Jesus mark the turning of the ages, “the end of the times,” after which God’s people live in the final stretch before His return (Hebrews 1:2; 9:26).

The phrase “for you” brings eternity down to a scattered group of congregations. The God who planned salvation before the world began did so with these very believers in view. Few thoughts could steady them more under the contempt of their neighbors than knowing that the Lamb was appointed, and then sent, for their sake.

wordNotes.term: προεγνωσμένου (proegnōsmenou) — foreordained
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “foreknown,” this participle shares its root with the foreknowledge of verse 2. Applied to Christ, it expresses God’s eternal purpose to give His Son as Redeemer, a purpose formed before creation and carried out in history.

wordNotes.term: φανερωθέντος (phanerōthentos) — was manifest
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to make visible what was previously hidden. Used of Christ, it presupposes His existence before His appearing in the flesh and highlights the incarnation as the disclosure of God’s eternal plan.

verses.bibleText: Who by him do believe in God, that raised him up from the dead, and gave him glory; that your faith and hope might be in God.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The readers are those “who by him do believe in God.” Christ is the way to the Father. Most of Peter’s readers had once served many gods; through Jesus they came to know the one true God, the God of Israel (1 Thessalonians 1:9-10). Christ reveals the Father’s character and opens access to Him (John 14:6, 9), so that faith in God and faith in Christ are bound together.

This God “raised him up from the dead, and gave him glory.” The resurrection and exaltation are the Father’s vindication of the Son. The One rejected by men was raised by God and crowned with honor at His right hand (Acts 2:32-36). The pattern announced in verse 11, sufferings followed by glory, has already come true for Christ.

The result follows: “that your faith and hope might be in God.” Because God raised Jesus, believers have every reason to trust Him with their own lives and future. The power that brought Christ out of the grave is the power that guards them now (v. 5) and will raise them at His coming. Faith looks back to what God has done, hope looks ahead to what He will do, and both rest on the same faithful God.

wordNotes.term: δόξαν αὐτῷ δόντα (doxan autō donta) — gave him glory
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase refers to the exaltation that followed the resurrection, when the Father publicly honored the Son. The glory Christ had with the Father before the world began was now displayed in His risen and ascended humanity.

verses.bibleText: Seeing ye have purified your souls in obeying the truth through the Spirit unto unfeigned love of the brethren, see that ye love one another with a pure heart fervently:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The fourth command concerns the life of the community. Peter first recalls what has already taken place: “Seeing ye have purified your souls in obeying the truth.” The perfect tense describes a past act with continuing effect. Purification was the vocabulary of Israel’s ritual cleansing before worship (Exodus 19:10; Numbers 8:21), and the New Testament applies it to the inward cleansing of heart and life (James 4:8; 1 John 3:3). Here it took place through obedience to the truth, the believing response to the gospel. To receive God’s truth is to submit to it; truth must be practiced as well as known. The Spirit who sanctifies (v. 2) is the One who makes that obedience possible.

The purpose of this purification was “unfeigned love of the brethren.” The term describes affection among siblings, the warmth of those who belong to one family. “Unfeigned” means without play-acting, the opposite of hypocrisy. Purity of life and sincerity of love belong together; a cleansed heart has room for others.

Then comes the command: “see that ye love one another with a pure heart fervently.” The verb now is the self-giving love that seeks another’s highest good. It must flow from a pure heart, free of mixed motives. And it must be fervent, a word that pictures something stretched out to its full extent, earnest and sustained without slackening. Such love reaches past the unattractive traits of others and keeps going when tested (4:8). In a hostile world, the church’s mutual love would be both a shelter for its members and a witness to those watching (John 13:35).

wordNotes.term: ἡγνικότες (hēgnikotes) — having purified
wordNotes.explanation: The verb, drawn from the language of ceremonial cleansing, came to describe moral and spiritual purification. The perfect tense marks a completed cleansing whose effect continues. Peter locates it in obedience to the truth, the heart’s surrender to the gospel.

wordNotes.term: φιλαδελφίαν ἀνυπόκριτον . . . ἐκτενῶς (philadelphian anypokriton . . . ektenōs) — unfeigned love of the brethren . . . fervently
wordNotes.explanation: Philadelphia denotes family affection among believers, and anypokritos means without pretense. The adverb ektenōs, used of the church’s earnest prayer for Peter in prison, describes love that is intense and unrelenting.

verses.bibleText: Being born again, not of corruptible seed, but of incorruptible, by the word of God, which liveth and abideth for ever.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The command to love rests on the new birth: “Being born again, not of corruptible seed, but of incorruptible.” Peter returns to the verb of verse 3. Believers love one another because they have been born into the same family by the same Father. Natural brothers and sisters share a common origin; Christians share a common birth from God.

The seed is “incorruptible.” Human birth comes from perishable seed and produces perishable life; every child of human parents will one day die. The new birth springs from another source and yields a life that death cannot finally destroy. Jesus told Nicodemus, “That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit” (John 3:6). The family formed by this birth will outlast every earthly tie, which gives the love practiced within it lasting significance.

The instrument is “the word of God, which liveth and abideth for ever.” In the parable of the sower Jesus identified the seed as the word of God sown in human hearts (Luke 8:11). When the gospel is preached and received, God’s word enters a life and begins to produce new life. James says the same: “Of his own will begat he us with the word of truth” (James 1:18). The Greek can be read as describing either the word or God as living and abiding. Both statements are true, and Scripture calls God’s word “quick, and powerful” because it carries the life of the One who speaks it (Hebrews 4:12).

This verse places Scripture at the center of conversion. People are not born again through religious feeling alone, through ritual, or through moral effort. The Spirit uses the word of God to bring them to life (v. 2). Apart from that word there is no regeneration; through it, anyone who receives it may be made new. The church’s ongoing health therefore depends on hearing, reading, and obeying the Scriptures, the same word that first gave it birth (2:2).

wordNotes.term: ἐκ σπορᾶς . . . ἀφθάρτου (ek sporas . . . aphthartou) — of incorruptible seed
wordNotes.explanation: Spora refers to seed or the act of sowing, the origin from which life springs. Aphthartos, already used of the inheritance in verse 4, marks this source as immune to decay. The new life believers receive shares the permanence of its origin.

wordNotes.term: διὰ λόγου ζῶντος θεοῦ καὶ μένοντος (dia logou zōntos theou kai menontos) — by the word of God, which liveth and abideth
wordNotes.explanation: The preposition marks the word as the means of the new birth. The participles “living” and “abiding” may describe the word or God Himself; the context, which next quotes Isaiah on the enduring word, favors the word, though its life derives from God.

verses.bibleText: For all flesh is as grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of grass. The grass withereth, and the flower thereof falleth away:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter confirms the point with Isaiah 40:6-8. “All flesh is as grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of grass.” “Flesh” here means humanity in its natural frailty. In the dry climate of the eastern Mediterranean, grass sprang up green after the rains and turned brown within days once the hot wind blew. Its blossoms, the loveliest part, were the first to go.

“The grass withereth, and the flower thereof falleth away.” Every human achievement shares that fate: beauty, wealth, reputation, learning, and political power. Peter’s readers faced an empire that looked permanent, with its temples, legions, and imperial cult. Isaiah’s words cut it down to size. Rome’s splendor, like that of every power before it, was a flower of the field (Psalm 103:15-16).

For persecuted believers this is comfort rather than gloom. Those who scorned them would not have the last word. A life resting on human glory will fade, while a life born of God’s word will endure.

wordNotes.term: πᾶσα σὰρξ ὡς χόρτος (pasa sarx hōs chortos) — all flesh is as grass
wordNotes.explanation: Sarx here denotes human beings in their weakness and mortality, not the sinful nature. Chortos is the wild grass of open fields. The simile, common in the Psalms and wisdom writings, stresses the brevity of human life and glory.

verses.bibleText: But the word of the Lord endureth for ever. And this is the word which by the gospel is preached unto you.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“But the word of the Lord endureth for ever.” Isaiah’s oracle closes with its great contrast: everything human withers, while what God speaks remains. In its first setting the passage opened a message of comfort for exiles in Babylon, promising that God would come to deliver His people and lead them home like a shepherd (Isaiah 40:1-11). Peter’s readers, exiles of another kind, receive the same assurance.

God’s promises never need revision. What He has declared about sin, salvation, and the coming kingdom stands as firmly as His own being (Matthew 24:35).

The apostle then makes the identification explicit: “this is the word which by the gospel is preached unto you.” Isaiah’s everlasting word is the gospel these believers heard from their evangelists (v. 12). The message of Christ crucified, risen, and returning is no passing religious idea. It belongs to the word of the Lord that abides forever. Those born of it share its permanence, and their love for one another, rooted in it, will last as well.

wordNotes.term: τὸ ῥῆμα κυρίου μένει εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα (to rhēma kyriou menei eis ton aiōna) — the word of the Lord endureth for ever
wordNotes.explanation: Rhēma denotes a spoken word or message. Peter uses it twice in this verse, linking the word Isaiah proclaimed with the gospel preached to his readers. The verb menō, “remain,” affirms that God’s declarations stand without alteration.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: What gives a person steady hope when faith in Christ makes him feel like a foreigner among the people he grew up with?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: God has begotten His people again to a living hope through the risen Christ, and that hope calls them to holy, reverent, loving lives while they wait for His appearing.
discussionQuestions: How does Peter hold together God’s foreknowledge and the believer’s obedient response in verse 2?
Why does Peter compare tested faith with refined gold, and what makes faith more precious?
What do verses 10-12 teach about the unity of the prophets’ message and the gospel?
How does knowing the cost of redemption shape the way a believer passes the time of sojourning?
Why does Peter connect the new birth with love for fellow believers?
commonMisunderstandings: Election according to foreknowledge is not an arbitrary decree that fixes destinies apart from faith and obedience.
Rejoicing in trials does not mean pretending that grief is absent or that suffering is good in itself.
Being kept by God’s power does not make faith unnecessary; God guards His people through their continuing trust.
The call to holiness is not a ladder for earning salvation but the family likeness of those already born again.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep the order of the chapter: God’s mercy, Christ’s resurrection and blood, and the Spirit’s work come first, and the commands to hope, holiness, reverence, and love grow out of them.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Fix your hope on the grace that Jesus will bring at His appearing, and let the price He paid move you to live as a holy, loving child of the Father today.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: Through the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ, God redeems people from an empty way of life and gives them new birth into a living hope.
flow: Every human life without God is fading like grass and caught in an empty inherited way of living.
God, in abundant mercy, provided a spotless Lamb chosen before the foundation of the world.
Christ’s precious blood ransoms sinners, and His resurrection gives a living hope.
Through the living word of God a person is born again and brought into God’s family.
The new life looks for Christ’s return and shows itself in holiness and love.
simpleIllustrations: A prisoner of war set free by a costly exchange does not go back to the camp; the price paid tells him what his freedom is worth.
Gold placed in a furnace loses only what is worthless, and comes out showing its real value.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you receive the life God offers through the risen Christ and let His precious blood redeem you from your old way of living?
cautions: Do not suggest that a believer’s security rests on a single past decision apart from continuing faith.
Do not present suffering as proof of God’s displeasure or as a price that buys salvation.
Do not reduce the new birth to moral improvement; it is God’s work through His word and Spirit.

reflectionQuestions: Where do I feel most like a stranger because I belong to Christ, and how does Peter’s greeting change how I see that?
What trial is presently testing my faith, and what might God be proving and refining through it?
Is my hope set fully on the grace Jesus will bring at His appearing, or partly on things that fade?
Which inherited habits or empty patterns from my former life still shape me, and how does the price of my redemption speak to them?
Whom in the family of faith do I find hardest to love fervently, and what would a pure-hearted love look like toward that person?
